anomaly_def.Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly: Static mismatch between physical data model (tables, indexes, partitions, data types, constraints) and the workload’s access patterns, forcing the optimizer into sub-optimal, scan-heavy plans and inflating maintenance work on writes. 
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly: Saturation of the underlying storage subsystem’s bandwidth, IOPS, or latency budget, causing elevated I/O wait times even when the database engine is issuing requests efficiently. 
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly: Exhaustion or near-exhaustion of allocated disk or file-system space for data, temp, or log areas, leading to allocation failures, halted growth, and stalled background maintenance.

When these three root causes coexist, the database exhibits compounding symptoms: 1) poorly indexed or non-partitioned tables trigger large table and index scans, dramatically inflating read and write volumes; 2) the excess I/O quickly pushes the storage array to its throughput limits, producing long device queues, rising read/write latencies, and session wait events; 3) the bloated access patterns and excessive spill-to-disk operations consume free space rapidly, filling data, temp, or log areas, which in turn causes auto-extend failures, out-of-space errors, and stalled checkpoints or archive writes. Performance degradation becomes erratic—queries oscillate between slow and failing outright—while maintenance tasks such as index rebuilds, backups, or purge jobs cannot complete due to both bandwidth starvation and lack of space.

Causally, an inefficient schema design inflates I/O volume, accelerating both throughput consumption and space usage. As the storage subsystem hits its throughput ceiling, operations slow, lengthening the time that temporary segments, inflated redo, and intermediate work areas remain on disk, which further depletes available space. Conversely, dwindling free space forces more frequent file-growth and log-switch events, amplifying write bursts and exacerbating the existing I/O bottleneck. The resulting feedback loop—poor design generating excess I/O, saturating bandwidth, which prolongs disk residency and hastens space exhaustion—creates a severe, self-reinforcing degradation of overall database performance and stability.

entry.official_description: Partitioned table '%s' is not allowed to use shared tablespace '%s'. Please move all partitions to file-per-table tablespaces before upgrade.
entry.cause_analysis: The failure is typically associated with file creation, filesystem access, write durability, log persistence, tablespace management, or storage-capacity boundaries.
entry.solution_guidance: Inspect filesystem capacity and permissions, verify persistence paths, review log and data placement, and check whether storage latency or write failures are affecting the engine.
